messages.content:
You are a performance diagnostician. You are given real measurements from a
running Spring Boot endpoint. Your job is to work out WHERE THE TIME ACTUALLY GOES
and deliver ranked, falsifiable hypotheses.

RULES — these are not negotiable:

1. The numbers below are MEASURED FACTS from a recorded benchmark run. You must not
   contradict them, restate them differently, or explain them away. If your theory
   disagrees with a number, your theory is wrong.
2. You must produce AT LEAST 3 COMPETING hypotheses spanning AT LEAST 2 different
   layers. Three restatements of one idea will be rejected by code.
3. You must RUN PROBES BEFORE RANKING. Ranking without experiments is guessing.
   Each probe you report must declare which hypotheses it separates.
4. Do not do arithmetic on raw samples — the derived facts below are already computed.
   Quote them.

=== MEASURED EVIDENCE (facts — do not contradict these) ===

Endpoint: GET /api/customers/bios
Run: 100 measured requests, 20 warmup discarded, corpus 742c1a719ba3c80d

LATENCY (ms, percentiles from raw samples)
       n       p50       p95       p99      mean     stdev
     100       5.7       9.6      22.7       6.7       3.6
  response statuses: {'200': 100}

TOP 1 APPLICATION SQL DIGESTS (by total time)
   calls  calls/req  total ms  mean ms  rows exam  no idx  sql
     100       1.00      25.1    0.251      20000       -  SELECT `cp1_0` . `id` , `cp1_0` . `customer_name` , `cp1_0` . `bio` FROM `customer_prof…

DERIVED FACTS (computed in Python from the recorded run)
  application SQL statements per request : 1.0
  total application SQL statements       : 100
  server-side SQL time                   : 39.8 ms  of 671.3 ms measured
  SQL share of measured latency          : 5.92 %
  NOT explained by SQL                   : 94.08 %
  rows examined / rows sent by MySQL     : 20000 / 10000
  digests reporting no index used        : 0

CANDIDATE N+1 (digests executing more than once per request)
  none — no digest executes more than once per request

CALL CHAIN (from the comprehension model)
  1. CustomerBioController.bios  (src/main/java/com/ex/web/CustomerBioController.java:21)  — controller method returns bios DTO list
  2. CustomerBioService.bios  (src/main/java/com/ex/service/CustomerBioService.java:22)  — service validates page size and calls repository
  3. CustomerProfileRepository.findBioRows  (src/main/java/com/ex/repo/CustomerProfileRepository.java:24)  — repository executes JPQL query returning DTOs

DECLARED DATA ACCESS
  [per req ] jpql_query  repo.findBioRows  (src/main/java/com/ex/repo/CustomerProfileRepository.java:24)

=== THE OPEN QUESTION — THIS IS THE WHOLE TASK ===

Server-side SQL accounts for only 5.92% of measured latency.
That means 94.08% of the time — the large majority — is spent SOMEWHERE ELSE,
and nothing in the SQL evidence tells you where.

The cost is an unknown cost per result row. A request returning zero rows is fast; a request returning
a few rows is slow. So something expensive happens PER RESULT ROW, and it is mostly
not the database.

Your central task: determine what that 94.08% is.

Do not assume it is the N+1 queries. The N+1 is real and visible above, but the SQL
timings say those queries account for a small fraction of the total. If you rank the
N+1 first, you must justify it against the 5.92% figure with evidence.

Candidate directions worth separating (do not just accept one):
  - work done per row in application code (loops, allocation, collection building)
  - ORM hydration: how many entity objects are materialised per row
  - serialization: how large the response is and what it costs to build the JSON
  - the database queries themselves

=== HOW TO EXPERIMENT ===

run_probe fires ONE OF THIS ENDPOINT'S OWN CORPUS REQUESTS, repeatedly, and reports
p50 latency, application SQL statements per request, server-side SQL ms per request,
result row count and RESPONSE BODY SIZE IN BYTES. It cannot call any other endpoint.

This endpoint's own requests, available to probe:
  dense-req-p0-s100: GET /api/customers/bios?page=0&size=100 — generated: path/query params from the comprehension model; page depth 0, page size 100
  dense-req-p2-s100: GET /api/customers/bios?page=2&size=100 — generated: path/query params from the comprehension model; page depth 2, page size 100

This endpoint paginates (max page size 100). Start by SWEEPING page_size: 1, a typical size, and the max. That tells you whether cost scales linearly with the number of result rows, and which quantities scale with it -- latency, SQL statements, SQL ms, or response bytes. Quantities that scale together are candidates for the same cause; quantities that stay flat are ruled out. Use iterations=3 for larger page sizes; they are slow.

For MECHANISM, use the call chain and the declared data access above — they tell you
which method runs per row and what it touches. State the mechanism in terms of what
that code does to each row, and tie it to a quantity your probes measured.

=== WHEN YOU ARE DONE ===

Call emit_hypotheses. Requirements enforced by code:
  - at least 3 hypotheses, spanning at least 2 different layers
  - layer must be one of: database_query, orm_hydration, application_logic, serialization, network, other
  - sum of attributed_ms must not exceed 7 ms
    (measured p50 is 5.7 ms, 20% tolerance)
  - ranked_ids must list every hypothesis id, most significant first
  - probes_run must contain at least one real probe with discriminates_between set

Do not write a prose report. Call emit_hypotheses.

messages.reasoning:
We need to run probes. Use run_probe to sweep page sizes. We have two request IDs: dense-req-p0-s100 and dense-req-p2-s100. Both default page size 100. We can override page_size param. Let's probe page size 1 and 100 for both depth maybe.

We want to see latency scaling. Run probe with page_size=1 on dense-req-p0-s100. iterations maybe 10. Then with page_size=100. Also maybe page_size=50. But limited probes.

We need discriminates_between list: which hypotheses each probe helps distinguish.

We haven't defined hypotheses yet; but we can plan: likely hypotheses:

h1: ORM hydration per row dominates (materializing DTOs). Layer orm_hydration. Attribution maybe 3 ms.

h2: JSON serialization per row dominates. Layer serialization. Attribution maybe 2 ms.

h3: Application logic per row (e.g., building list, mapping) dominates. Layer application_logic. Attribution maybe 1 ms.

Sum <=7ms. p50 5.7ms, tolerance 20% -> 6.84ms max total attribution. We'll allocate 3+2+1 =6 ms fits.

Now need probes to separate. If latency scales linearly with row count, could be any per-row cost. Need differentiate between orm_hydration vs serialization vs other. Perhaps response body size scales with rows (serialization cost). We can look at response body size from probe results.

If latency scales but response body size also scales linearly, then serialization likely. If latency scales but body size is small, maybe ORM.

We can also look at SQL statements per request remain 1.0 irrespective of rows. That's already known.

We can also maybe use explain? Not needed.

We'll run two probes: size 1 and size 100. Then examine latency and response size.

Let's run.

function.description:
Run a live experiment against THIS RUN'S OWN ENDPOINT and measure what happens. Fires one of this endpoint's own corpus requests `iterations` times, resets and re-reads performance_schema around the measured calls, and reports p50 latency, application SQL statements per request, server-side SQL ms per request, result row count and response body size.

This is READ-ONLY and cannot call any other endpoint, verb or body shape — only the requests this run's own corpus already generated for the endpoint under test.

Caps: iterations at most 20 (clamped, not rejected). page_size at most 100 (clamped).
function.name: run_probe

page_size.description: Override this request's own page size, 1 to 100. Sweep it to find out whether cost scales with the number of result rows. Omit to use the request's own recorded size unchanged.

request_id.description:
Which of this endpoint's own corpus requests to fire, repeatedly. Each id varies this endpoint's own real magnitude (a denser or sparser path parameter, a deeper page) — the same requests the benchmark phase itself uses, not an invented one. Available ids and what they are:
  dense-req-p0-s100: GET /api/customers/bios?page=0&size=100 — generated: path/query params from the comprehension model; page depth 0, page size 100
  dense-req-p2-s100: GET /api/customers/bios?page=2&size=100 — generated: path/query params from the comprehension model; page depth 2, page size 100

function.description: Call this ONCE, after running probes, to deliver your diagnosis. This is the only way to finish. Your submission is checked by code: if a check fails you will be told exactly what is wrong and must fix it and call this again.
function.name: emit_hypotheses

hypotheses.description: At least 3 COMPETING explanations, spanning at least 2 different layers. Not one theory restated three ways.

attributed_ms.description: How many ms of the measured p50 this explains. The sum across all hypotheses must fit inside p50.

claim.description: What is slow, in one sentence.

evidence.description: Specific numbers from the measured evidence or from your probe results, quoted. Not general reasoning.

layer.description: Which layer the time is spent in.

mechanism.description: WHY that costs time — the specific chain of cause and effect, citing code where you read it.

prediction.description: A testable statement that would be FALSE if this hypothesis is wrong.

probes_run.description: Every probe you actually ran, and what it settled.

discriminates_between.description: Hypothesis ids this probe separates. A probe that separates nothing is not an experiment.

result.description: What it measured and what it ruled in or out.

ranked_ids.description: All hypothesis ids, most significant first. Rank by attributed ms supported by evidence, not by how familiar the cause is.

function.description: EXPLAIN ANALYZE a SELECT against the real database: the plan with ACTUAL rows and ACTUAL timings, plus the access type per table, rows examined versus rows returned, and whether any index was used. This runs the query — it is a measurement, not an estimate.
function.name: explain

params.description: Values for the %s placeholders, in order.

sql.description: One SELECT statement. Use %s for parameters.

function.description: Every index on a table, with its columns IN ORDER, whether it is unique, its cardinality and its size on disk. Column order decides which filters an index can serve, so read it before proposing anything.
function.name: list_indexes
